drills.title: vs Vijay-malu (823) — Three Knights Opening
drills.coachNote: White's knight on e5 is eyeing g6, a square that attacks both your queen on e7 and your rook on f8 in one move — a fork you need to prevent, not invite. Your f6 attacks the knight but doesn't stop it from jumping anyway: after Ng6 your queen has to run (Qf7), then Nxf8 snaps up the rook and Rxf8 recaptures — you handed back a knight-for-rook swing, nearly four pawns of value. Rfe8 solves it at the root by taking the rook off f8 before the fork can land; after Nf3 Qd7 Qd2 Rxe1+ Rxe1 you're simply safe. Always check what square the enemy knight wants next, not just what it's doing now.

drills.coachNote: d4 looks tempting as a central outpost, but White's knight on f3 and pawn on d3 both watch that square, so anything landing there is simply hanging, not threatening anything. You played Nd4 and White just took it: Nxd4, and after exd4 recaptures you're down a full piece for nothing, with the queen swinging to g4 keeping you busy while material behind. Ne7 instead keeps the knight safe and flexible, eyeing c6 and d5, and after c4 g6 Qb3 Rb8 d4 you're still in a normal, solid game. Before jumping a piece to a 'nice' central square, count exactly who defends and attacks it.

drills.title: vs belyjudegwapo (730) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: You're already up over four pawns here, and White's bishop on e4 is completely undefended — no pawn, no piece covers it. Bd7 doesn't touch that bishop at all; it just retreats quietly and lets White play d4, striking your e5 pawn, and after exd4 Nxd4 Re8 White fights back into the center while your huge edge shrinks by three pawns' worth. d5 was the move: it hits the loose bishop on e4 directly, and even if White tries the desperate Bxh7+ Kxh7 Nxe5 Bxe5 Bxe5 sacrifice, the dust settles with you still comfortably ahead. When you're winning big, don't just develop — check if something's simply hanging first.

drills.coachNote: Before you recapture, notice White's rook sits on f1 with the entire first rank empty in front of it — your bishop on a1 is completely undefended. Kxf8 grabs the piece back on f8 but ignores that, and White simply plays Rxa1 next, picking up your stray bishop for free and clawing back almost two pawns of your huge lead. Bd4+ fixes the move order: the check forces Kh1 first, so White's rook never gets the free tempo to swing over, and only then do you play Kxf8 — after Nxf4 Bf5 c3 you're still dominating, just without the giveaway. When several of your pieces are loose, find the check that buys you time before you recapture.

drills.coachNote: Black's dark-squared bishop on h6 is pointed straight at your bishop on g5 — that trade is sitting there for Black to take on his turn. Bh4 sidesteps the attack entirely, keeping your bishop active and out of reach, and after Rg8 Nbd2 Bh3 Bg3 Bg4 you keep maneuvering with the bishop pair intact instead of simplifying into an easier position for Black. When a piece is attacked, move it before you do anything else.

drills.coachNote: White's pawn on e4 can shove straight to e5, attacking whatever lands on f6 with tempo, while the queen on f3 is already staring down the f-file at f7. drills.coachNote: You're winning massively here, and White's king on e1 is still undeveloped — a check forces more concessions because there's nothing better for White to do. Qe5 retreats the queen passively instead of pressing that, and it gives White a free tempo: a3 and f4 kick your queen around (Qe4 forced), clawing back a pawn and a half of your edge while White tidies up. Bb4+ keeps the pressure where it belongs: it forces Nc3 as the only block, then Bxc3+ bxc3 Qxc3+ grabs another pawn with check, and Kf2 leaves you still dictating every move. When the enemy king hasn't moved and can't easily shelter, look for the check before you look for a quiet move.

drills.coachNote: Black's knight on c6 has exactly one defender, the queen on d6, and that queen and the bishop on e6 sit a single pawn-push apart from your pawn on d4. Ng6 goes chasing a different idea entirely, and it lets Black play Rf6 hitting your knight, with Nxf5 Bxf5 Bf4 following — you give back your whole 2.8-pawn edge and then some. Nxc6 was the move: trading knight for knight first, and after Qxc6 recaptures, d5 forks the queen on c6 and the bishop on e6 — the queen has to run (Qe8), and dxe6 just takes the bishop for free, leaving you up a clean piece after Rd8. When two enemy pieces sit a pawn-push apart, trade off the defender and let the fork collect the second.

drills.coachNote: Black's knight on f4 is ready to jump into e2 or d3, squares that slice your king away from the queenside, while his bishop on e5 is simply waiting to scoop up c3. Marching your king to e4 does nothing about either idea — after Ne2 your king was already cut off, and when you pushed on with Kd5 anyway, Bxc3 and Bf2 followed, swinging a roughly equal ending (+0.2) into a lost one. Instead, Be4 enters the race from the other side: after Ke6 Bb7 Nd5 Bxa6, yes c3 still falls, but your bishop grabs a6 right back, keeping the pawns level. In piece endings, let your pieces run the race — don't send the king where the knight can exploit it.

Resolving it with cxd3 instead flips the tension in your favor: after Ng3, dxc2+ is a discovered pawn fork with check, and after Qxc2 Rxd1+ Rxd1 you've traded favorably and come out ahead.
